solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Being in the Police is the pinnacle of rock

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a French police officer, someone serving in the force
second meaning: a mountaineering term for a rock tower standing on a ridge

explanation.surface: Being a member of the band The Police is the very top of rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: The Police were a famous rock band, which makes 'pinnacle of rock' read like praise of them; both halves are separate meanings, one from policing and one from climbing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a French armed policeman, and climbers borrowed it for a rocky spire blocking a ridge, as if guarding it.

clue.text: Beastly type in a rage with pet barking

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go crazy and rearrange

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A furious animal sits beside a yapping household dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like what the pet is doing, but in British slang it means mad, signalling the shuffle; 'with' simply joins the two pieces of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorillas, chimpanzees and orangutans are large primates, literally beasts, so a 'beastly type' is a playful way of describing one.

clue.text: Material used to make many longhouses

indicators.note: the letters needed go to make up part of the following words, sitting inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Some fabric was used in building a lot of traditional longhouses.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests building supplies, but the answer sits in plain sight across 'many' and 'longhouses'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a synthetic fabric used for clothing, rope and stockings, so it is a material in the textile sense.

clue.text: Government bill pint-sized Republican put in post

parts.note: an ad is a bill or poster advertising something
mini means very small

indicators.note: putting something in another means placing it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a station is a post, as in a duty station
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A government proposal concerns a short Republican appointed to a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like legislation to go with 'Government', but it is an advert; R is the usual abbreviation for a Republican in US politics.
explanation.definitionFit: The governing team in power, especially in the US, is called the Administration, so it stands for a government.

clue.text: Flapper in raincoat that's adorable

parts.note: a mac (mackintosh) is a British word for a raincoat
aw is the cooing sound people make at something cute

explanation.surface: A 1920s flapper girl looks sweet in her raincoat.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper suggests a jazz-age young woman, but here it is anything that flaps its wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A large parrot is a bird, and birds flap their wings, so the setter calls it a flapper in a playful literal sense.

clue.text: Bishop in drink coming over? Help!

indicators.note: coming over suggests turning or flipping, so the word is read back to front
in places one thing within another, so a letter sits inside

parts.note: tea is a drink
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop drinking at a gathering gets dizzy and cries for help.
explanation.walkthrough: TEA turned round gives AET, and B sits after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to assist or encourage, usually in wrongdoing, so it works as a verb meaning to give someone a hand.

clue.text: A pretty mischievous feature in a church

parts.note: taken as written
cute means pretty or attractive
arch means playfully mischievous or knowing

explanation.surface: A charming, impish detail is found inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty mischievous' reads as 'quite naughty', with pretty as an adverb, but each word is a separate adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharply pointed arch, typical of Gothic architecture, is a common structural element of church buildings.

clue.text: English country houses

definitions.note: plural clue word for a collective noun: one estate is many houses

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a state is a country or nation

explanation.surface: Grand stately homes in the English countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country houses' looks like one phrase meaning stately homes, but 'country' belongs to the wordplay and 'houses' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A housing estate is a planned development of many homes built together, so a group of dwellings.

clue.text: I'm right to tell new nurses medics' ultimately useful info

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold and cradle, so one piece is held within the other
a new version of the words means their letters are made into something different

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone insists they are correct to brief newly qualified nurses on information doctors find handy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New nurses' reads as freshly qualified nurses, but 'new' is the anagram signal and 'nurses' a verb; S sits inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means anything that can be turned to profit or advantage, like grain brought for grinding, so helpful material.

clue.text: Live with line-snorting mum, creating this?

definitions.text: Live with line-snorting mum, creating this
definitions.note: the whole clue describes the chaos that would result

parts.note: to be is to live or exist

indicators.note: snorting something draws it up inside, so one piece is taken into another

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Sharing a home with a mother who snorts lines of cocaine would cause uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in full, the clue describes a household in turmoil, which is exactly the answer; 'mum' is an animal's mother, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a notorious London asylum became a general word for wild noisy chaos, which such a home would produce.

clue.text: My periods of sexual activity enthral quiet doctors

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: to enthral is literally to hold captive, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: the rut is the mating season of deer and similar animals
p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that their randy spells captivated some silent physicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' looks like a noun for physicians, but it is the verb meaning tampers with; 'My' is an exclamation, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: To doctor something is to falsify or tamper with it, and to corrupt is likewise to alter it dishonestly.

clue.text: School memo written in a quasi-Arabic style

indicators.note: Arabic script runs from right to left, so the word is set down backwards

parts.note: a note is a short memo

explanation.surface: A school memo is written in an imitation Arabic script.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like calligraphy, but the point is only the direction of writing: right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is the famous English boys' public school near Windsor, a crossword staple for 'school'.

clue.text: Son breaks fresh coverage of fake ghosts in bulletins

parts.note: fresh means new

indicators.note: something that breaks into a phrase splits it and sits in the gap

parts.note: a cartoon or fancy-dress ghost is a person under a bedsheet
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A son breaks a story with fresh reports of hoax ghost sightings in the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' sounds journalistic, but it means what covers a fake ghost, the bedsheet of fancy dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A single printed page of news or announcements is a news sheet, so it serves as a published bulletin.

clue.text: Court reporter maybe displays subpoena in front of the Queen

parts.note: to sport something is to wear or display it
a subpoena is a writ ordering someone to court
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A court stenographer shows a subpoena in front of the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court reporter' and 'subpoena' point to a law court, but the court is a tennis court; 'maybe' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist covering tennis reports on matches played on court, and is one kind of sports journalist.

clue.text: Big brat in for treatment, being very gassy

indicators.note: treatment works on something and changes it, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A large spoilt child is admitted to hospital for severe flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gassy' suggests wind, but it means talkative. 'Rabbit on' is British slang for chattering endlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Gassy can mean full of idle talk, and rabbiting means chattering on at length, so both describe a windbag.

clue.text: Bloody freezing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: uncooked and red, as underdone meat
second meaning: bitterly cold and damp, of weather

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as the British expletive 'bloody freezing', meaning very cold, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Underdone meat is described as bloody or uncooked, and a bitter chill in the air is called a cold, biting day.

clue.text: Dame exercising with a tin full of beans

indicators.note: exercising works and moves things about, so the letters are put through their paces into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An older lady works out holding a can of baked beans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin full of beans' paints a can of beans, but 'full of beans' is a separate idiom serving as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of beans is an idiom for being lively and energetic, which is just what an animated person is.

clue.text: Full of cold, writhing feverishly with bad twitching

indicators.note: being full of something means holding it inside
doing something feverishly is frantic and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone with a heavy cold is squirming in fever, twitching badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitching' looks like a feverish symptom, but in Britain twitching is the hobby of chasing rare birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Twitching is British slang for the hobby of chasing sightings of rare species of birds, a keen form of observing wildlife.

clue.text: Harshly ridicule a trip in tub for all to hear

indicators.note: something meant for everyone to hear is spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a tub is slang for a boat, and a trip in one is a sail

explanation.surface: Someone mocks another's boating excursion loudly in public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tub' suggests a bath, but it is slang for a slow, clumsy boat.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail is to attack, including with words, so savage criticism or mockery is a verbal assault.

clue.text: A hand in seas cast adrift

indicators.note: something adrift floats loose and wanders, so the letters drift out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor is set adrift at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand' reads as a deckhand and 'cast adrift' as one phrase, but 'cast' belongs to the letters to be rearranged and 'a hand' means help.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone a hand means helping them, so a hand is a piece of help or support.

clue.text: Dig not being clobbered around head in Glasgow

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece goes outside another

parts.note: clobber is British slang for clothes, so unclothed

indicators.note: the head of a word is its beginning, so its first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the city

explanation.surface: A jab in a Glasgow street fight leaves someone unbeaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobbered' looks like beaten up, but clobber is British slang for clothes, so 'not being clobbered' means undressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dig in the ribs is a poke with the elbow, the same small push of the arm or finger.

clue.text: Dumb artist medium-sized record label rejected

parts.note: M is the clothing size label for medium

indicators.note: rejected suggests thrown back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: EMI is a famous British record company

explanation.surface: A foolish, mid-ranking musician is dropped by the record company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dumb' suggests stupid, but here it means silent, as in performing without speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who acts out stories through gesture alone, never speaking, is a silent entertainer.

clue.text: I filled canvas bag with Medical Officer at front

definitions.note: the answer speaking in the first person

parts.note: MO is the abbreviation for Medical Officer
a net is a mesh bag, as for shopping

explanation.surface: Someone stuffed a canvas holdall with a military doctor sitting at its front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canvas bag' looks like one item, but the break comes after 'canvas': the painter speaks, and 'bag' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Monet was the French Impressionist painter who covered many canvases with water lilies and haystacks.

clue.text: Worker provided with stock of various kinds

parts.note: a man is a worker, as in workman or manpower
if means provided that
a stock phrase is a well-worn, old one

explanation.surface: An employee is supplied with goods of assorted types.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provided with stock' reads as being supplied with goods, but 'provided' is the conjunction meaning 'on condition that'.
explanation.definitionFit: Manifold describes something with many different forms or parts, so it means diverse and numerous.

clue.text: Light infantryman must retreat by dark, according to message

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
text-message spelling of the word for darkness after sunset

explanation.surface: A lightly armed soldier is ordered by message to fall back after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light infantryman' reads as one military term, but 'Light' is the definition; 'according to message' marks the texting spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To light a fire or fuse is to set it burning, so the verb means to kindle or set alight.

clue.text: Journal left in toilet

indicators.note: in places one thing within another, so a letter sits inside

parts.note: bog is British slang for a toilet
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A diary is left behind in the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a past tense of leaving, but it is the abbreviation L; bog is British slang for a lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: A web log is an online diary of posts, so it is a modern kind of personal journal.

clue.text: Collapsed apartment needs action to secure it

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: a deed is an action
flat is the British word for an apartment

explanation.surface: A building whose flat has fallen in needs urgent work to make it safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapsed apartment' reads as one phrase about a ruined home, but 'Collapsed' alone is the definition; 'it' points back to the apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deflated has had the air let out, so it has sagged and fallen in on itself like a punctured balloon.
